Title: Viral video raises questions over safety of green-painted motorcycle lane
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A viral video showing several motorcyclists apparently losing control on a rain-soaked green-painted section of the Federal Highway motorcycle lane near Subang has raised questions over its safety in wet weather.
The 42-second video, shared on Threads, shows several motorcycles lying on the lane, with some riders seen at the roadside.
The footage also shows the wet painted section, while other motorcyclists appear to slow down as they approach and pass through the area.
The location is believed to be the Federal Highway motorcycle lane near Subang, Selangor.
According to the post accompanying the video, the incident allegedly occurred during rainfall and was the second such incident at the location.
However, the exact date of the incident and the condition of the riders involved could not be independently verified.
The footage has prompted questions over whether the painted surface provides sufficient grip in wet conditions, although there is no confirmation that it contributed to the reported falls.
The Federal Highway motorcycle lane near Subang had previously drawn attention over the use of green-painted sections at several points along the route.
In August, the Public Works Department (PWD) was reported to have said the surface at the Subang exit was a localised treatment implemented based on engineering considerations and with the approval of the relevant authorities.
The treatment was intended to highlight areas with a higher risks, including bends and exit lanes, and alert motorcyclists to exercise greater caution.
Motorcyclists using the route had also previously raised concerns about how the painted surface performed during rainy weather.

Title: Haze worsens in Serian, schools closed
Article:
KUCHING: The air pollution index (API) in Serian worsened, exceeding the very unhealthy level this morning.
The Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System recorded an API reading of 221 in Serian as of 6am, placing it in the very unhealthy category.
As a result, all primary and secondary schools under the Serian District Education Office have been temporarily closed today.
The Sarawak Education Department said in a statement last night that the decision was made to ensure the health, safety and wellbeing of students and school staff following worsening haze in the district near the Malaysia-Indonesia border.
Home-based teaching and learning will be conducted.
Other districts that recorded unhealthy API readings were Kuching (194), Samarahan (188), Bintulu (170), Sri Aman (168), Samalaju (164), Sarikei (160),
Sibu (159), Mukah (155) and Miri (148).
For schools located near districts where API readings exceed 200, headteachers have been advised to consider implementing home-based teaching and learning.
An API reading of zero to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, and above 300 hazardous.

Title: Oil up almost two pct as Iran's president vows to never surrender
Article:
HOUSTON: Oil prices were up almost two per cent a barrel on Wednesday in choppy trade, as traders evaluated Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's vow never to surrender, a day after US President Donald Trump warned he could "annihilate" Iran.
Brent crude futures rose US$1.84, or 1.85per cent, to US$101.09 a barrel by 11:11 a.m. EDT while West Texas Intermediate futures gained 69 cents, or 0.76per cent, to US$91.two1.
At the UN General Assembly in New York, Pezeshkian said in a speech on Wednesday that Tehran would never surrender to the US but still believes in diplomacy. On Tuesday, Trump used a speech at the same forum to make his threat.
Tehran was reviewing the US response to its proposal to end hostilities, though many differences remain, a senior Iranian official told Reuters.
A reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and lifting of Washington's naval blockade on Iran were discussed during indirect talks on Tuesday, the official said.
Earlier on Wednesday, Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei had said the Strait of Hormuz would not be reopened while Iran's conditions are not met.
Meanwhile, European low-sulphur gasoil's premium to Brent crude futures hit a record of about US$95 a barrel after Trump said he backed the idea of a diesel export ban to lower prices that have hit record highs owing to a global supply shortage.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said later that a diesel export ban would not work. Analysts and market watchers have warned that such a move would do little to ease high energy prices and could worsen global supplies and further disrupt economies.
Europe has depended on diesel and jet fuel imports from the USduring the US-Israeli war on Iran.
"Brent is being underpinned by surging gasoil prices amid renewed worries the US may introduce a diesel export ban," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank.
Meanwhile, US crude inventories rose by three million barrels to 4two6.4 million barrels in the week ended September 18, the Energy Information Administration said. Analysts polled by Reuters had expected a 641,000-barrel draw. Fuel stocks fell.
RISING GULF SUPPLIES, DIPLOMACY HOPES
On Tuesday, the Brent benchmark hit its lowest since September 8 at US$97.36. Early on Wednesday, WTI touched its lowest since September 1. Prices were pressured by more supplies flowing out of the Middle East and hopes for a peace deal soon between Washington and Tehran.
Saudi Arabia resumed operations on its East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea on Tuesday, said three sources briefed on the matter.
"The only news that is worth focusing on from a lower price point is the reopening of the East-West Saudi pipeline," Hansen added.
Drone attacks, which Saudi Arabia has blamed on Iraqi militia, forced the kingdom to shut the pipeline on September 11, halting crude loadings at Yanbu port.
On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia offered more barrels to Asian refiners for lifting from locations outside of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iraq's minister said on Tuesday the country is exporting more than three million bpd, and expects to boost exports via Turkey to more than 600,000 barrels per day.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within seven days if the US eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that both Russia and Ukraine had expressed interest in a limited ceasefire involving grains and energy.
(Reporting by Georgina McCartney in Houston, Anushree Mukherjee and Enes Tunagur in London, Helen Clark in Perth and Siyi Liu in Singapore Editing by David Goodman and David Gregorio)

Title: Woman killed, five family members injured in Tanah Merah crash
Article:
KOTA BARU: A woman was killed while her husband and four children were injured in an accident involving their Perodua Alza and a Toyota Hilux at Jalan Rantau Panjang-Panglima Bayu, Tanah Merah, yesterday.
Tanah Merah district police chief Supt Mohd Haki Hasbullah said Tengku Ziarulwida Tuan Zainudin, 39, who was a passenger in the Perodua Alza, was killed on the spot in the 3pm incident.
He said preliminary investigations showed that the Perodua Alza, driven by Tengku Ziarulwida's husband, Mohd Saifulzawawi Ghani, 39, collided head-on with the Toyota Hilux.
The family was travelling from Rantau Panjang, Pasir Mas, towards Panglima Bayu.
"Mohd Saifulzawawi and two of his children were seriously injured and admitted to the Red Zone of Tanah Merah Hospital.
"The other two children are in the Yellow Zone," he said in a statement last night.
The Toyota Hilux driver, Che Ibrahim Che Min, 48, sustained minor injuries.
He said the case was being investigated under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987. — BERNAMA

Title: #NSTviral: Teacher's 16 weeks lesson plan reduced to soggy scraps
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Sixteen weeks of carefully prepared lesson plans were reduced to soggy scraps after a teacher's bag fell from her scooter, scattering her documents across a wet road and into the path of passing vehicles.
The practicum teacher, who goes by @arahhsn on Threads, said she had placed her bag on the scooter's footrest before it fell, scattering her stamped lesson plans and other paperwork.
"What a sad day. Sixteen weeks of lesson plans, which had already been stamped, were scattered and destroyed on the road.
"Luckily, I managed to save my teaching permit," she wrote.
She said she tried to collect the soaked papers to avoid leaving the road littered, with a passerby stopping to help.
"Thankfully, a kind person also helped me earlier. Thank you, kind stranger," she said.
She said the scattered papers were no longer there when she returned to the area at a later time.
The post has since garnered more than 580,000 views and over 10,000 likes, drawing responses from other users.
"What matters is that you're okay. The lesson plans can be printed again," @caramellatte1988 wrote.
"Get some rest first, okay? Tomorrow, start again. You can do it!" @alnnjwa_ wrote.
Another user wished her well in her practicum.
"I hope everything is made easier for you and that you get an A for your practicum," the user wrote.

Title: Australia says OpenAI agent hacked into government website
Article:
SYDNEY: Australia said on Wednesday an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal of a government agency responsible for non-sensitive health data and statistics, including public medical spending.
"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese said during a media briefing in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.
Investigations continue and Australia had voiced its "extreme concern about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company's delay in notifying the government.
"It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all," Albanese said, adding that the investigation would also examine why government systems had failed to detect the breach in the first place.
He also warned that three other government websites "may be impacted" by the OpenAI agent's activity.
"The question is, when it was trying to harvest data, did it go into these other sites? So we're not confirming that that occurred," he said.
The incident comes after OpenAI and Anthropic, in separate submissions to a parliamentary inquiry this month, urged Australia to reconsider a ban on use of the country's creative content to train their models.
'AI models attempted to look up answers'
"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names," OpenAI said in a statement.
It added that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend."
The Australian breach is the latest of several recent incidents in which OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorised activity involving its AI agents well after they occurred.
In some cases this was because the activity was only detected belatedly, and in others because the company initially elected not to disclose it.
A separate high-profile incident, a mid-July intrusion into open-source AI repository Hugging Face, was only detected about a week after it took place, according to timelines released by OpenAI and independent investigators.
This helped ignite global debate about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI models.
Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.
Some of America's top AI executives, including Altman, have called for a slowdown of industry development, citing, among other factors, the threat of devastating cyber attacks by out-of-control agents.

Title: 'There will be elections in Venezuela,' interim leader tells UN
Article:
United Nations, United States, Sept 24, 2026 (AFP) -
Venezuela's interim leader Delcy Rodriguez thanked US President Donald Trump for restoring diplomatic ties and told the United Nations on Wednesday that "there will be elections" in the Latin American country.
Rodriguez replaced president Nicolas Maduro following his ouster by US forces in January, and she has served as a pliant ally to Washington since then.
Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, she thanked the Trump administration "for their willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation with Venezuela."
"I want to state this very clearly before this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela," she added, without mentioning a timeline.
She did not refer to the US raid on Caracas that ousted her predecessor either, instead focusing on the transition to a "stage of democracy" in Venezuela.
Many Venezuelans were hopeful that ongoing, US-backed political transition talks between the interim government and parts of the opposition would lead to a democratic election.
But those hopes were dashed somewhat in early September when Trump, speaking shortly after striking a mega oil deal with Caracas, brushed off the notion of a vote in the near future.
Rodriguez echoed those comments at the time.
Her trip to New York has featured meetings with International Monetary Fund executives and several heads of state, including Trump.
The last Venezuelan leader to address the UN General Assembly was Maduro in 2018.

Title: Archaeological 'breakthrough' could confirm origins of Paris
Article:
PARIS: An ancient wall discovered in central Paris was hailed as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday, as the archaeological find may have settled a long-standing debate about the location of the city's original settlement.
A roughly 20-metre (66-foot) wall dating from the Gallo-Roman period was discovered in Paris this summer beneath a hospital on the Ile de la Cite, a stone's throw from Notre Dame Cathedral, the French culture ministry said.
The stone-and-wood find is thought to be a fragment of the ramparts of Lutetia – the ancient name for Paris – built by the Gallic Parisii tribe, which lived along the River Seine in the Iron Age.
The Ile de la Cite has traditionally been regarded as the centre of Lutetia, but a rival theory, backed by archaeological research, contends that it was actually in Nanterre, a suburb to the west.
"We may be looking at one of the most important remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia," Culture Minister Catherine Pegard said in a statement, which described the discovery as "a major breakthrough."
"Scientific caution still requires that we verify its function and its chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable at this stage."
Lutetia was first mentioned in Book Seven of Roman leader Julius Caesar's "Gallic Wars" series, where it was said to be on an island in the River Seine linked by bridges – a vague description that has given rise to many theories about its location.
[[nid:1539804]]
'Dizzying'
The wall, uncovered in the course of excavations beneath the Hotel-Dieu hospital, also bears traces of fire, which may correspond to Caesar's account that the Gauls set fire to their town before the Battle of Lutetia against the Romans.
Through carbon-dating technology, the charred evidence is estimated to date from 10-200 BC, the ministry said in its statement – a timeframe that includes the Battle of Lutetia in 52 BC.
The Ile de la Cite, home to Notre Dame Cathedral, is the largest island in the River Seine in the Paris region and became the centre of the Roman settlement of Lutetia.
"It's dizzying to find oneself here and to discover what is probably the origin of the city of Paris," Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said on Wednesday after examining the wall.
It is barely a metre high and had been buried four metres deep in a courtyard of the Hotel-Dieu hospital, which is the oldest in the capital.
An archaeological dig began there in February.
"All of our predecessors dreamed of finding traces of Gallic presences on the Ile de la Cite," said Dorothee Chaoui-Derieux, coordinator of archaeological operations in Paris for the culture ministry.
"There has been a lot of speculation on the subject. We're fortunate to be in the right place at the right time," she added.
"Beneath our feet, thanks to the trowels of our colleagues, this wall built in the Gallic tradition is gradually revealing its secrets."

Title: As five pct Treasury yields lose shock value, investors start worrying about six pct
Article:
LONDON: For years, five per cent on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield was viewed as the point at which global financial markets would start hitting turbulence.
That threshold is beginning to look less like a ceiling and more like a waypoint.
This month's breach of five per cent - something that has happened only briefly in recent decades - has forced investors to contemplate an unsettling question: What if six per cent is the new number that should be keeping them awake at night?
The latest move above five per cent has not lasted long enough yet to properly test that theory. But it has always been a psychological marker rather than an automatic tripwire, according to BlueBay Asset Management's head of market strategy, Mike Bell.
"People think of it as if there's a magic number for Treasury yields at which it becomes a problem, (but) it's a relative number, not an absolute number," Bell explained.
What matters is how Treasury yields compare with other key investment metrics, particularly the earnings yield on stocks. Bell says that relationship is now approaching an inflection point, potentially setting the stage for an equity selloff.
History offers some guidance. MSCI's main world stocks index halved in value the last time the 10-year Treasury yield broke five per cent, which was just before the global financial crash. It suffered a similar slump less than a decade earlier when a near six.8 per cent spike helped pop the dotcom bubble.
JP Morgan's analysts say one of the reasons why the pain-point might now be above five per cent again is a "key structural shift" in the global economy, with AI, healthcare and services playing a bigger role. Many of those firms are spending and expanding, regardless of the level of borrowing costs.
That means "the traditional interest-rate channel looks materially less binding" and the "breaking threshold" of stock markets may be "meaningfully higher, potentially in the five.five per cent-six.0 per cent range", JP Morgan said, referencing the views of some of the major investors at one of its most recent conferences.
PROFOUND REPRICING
In the US$29-trillion Treasury market, which anchors pricing for virtually all financial assets, a shift from five per cent to six per cent would represent a profound adjustment in the global cost of capital.
A six per cent Treasury yield would imply either significantly higher inflation expectations, growing concerns about US fiscal sustainability, a conviction that interest rates will remain elevated for years - or a mix of all three.
Federal Reserve policymaker Austan Goolsbee said this week that he didn't know whether markets would react differently to a lengthier period of five per cent yields than they had in the past.
Paul Jackson, Invesco global head of asset allocation research, said investors focus on Treasury yields for a simple reason: Treasuries represent the world's risk-free benchmark and at above five per cent, investors can lock in the highest returns on US bonds since 2007.
Jackson's own calculations show world stocks start to drop when the 10-year yield has traded at an average of 4.72 per cent for 12 months and then rises.
That tipping point remains some way off for now - the 12-month average is currently around 4.34 per cent - but Jackson said he was already dialling back on stocks and switching some money into government bonds to cash in on the juicy yields.
"If Treasury yields keep rising then there is a risk that the stock market is lower in 12 months' time," he said.
EMERGING QUESTIONS
Emerging markets, which have enjoyed something of a hot streak in recent years, are often among the first casualties when US yields surge.
Higher Treasury returns tend to strengthen the dollar and make dollar-denominated assets more attractive. That sucks capital away from EM economies and can tip hard-up countries into crisis if the cost of servicing their dollar-denominated debt spirals.
Data on investment flows shows last week saw the biggest exodus from EM bond funds in months, with billions also withdrawn from equity funds. Issuance of emerging-market sovereign debt has also been notably lighter than usual this month.
"It's not an optimal picture for EM," said Alison Shimada, Head of Total Emerging Markets Equity, Allspring Global Investments, although she stressed that for now nothing was going "horribly wrong" and therefore remained "constructive".
Perhaps the biggest risk is psychological.
Once investors start asking whether six per cent is attainable, the debate shifts beyond a temporary spike in yields. It becomes a broader reckoning with the possibility that the era of abundant liquidity and ultra-cheap money has ended, forcing global asset prices to adapt to a permanently higher cost of capital.
Premier Miton CIO Neil Birrell said while stock markets were showing no sign of collapsing right now, that might be because investors weren't yet plugging in five per cent-plus yields into their longer-term profit forecasting models.
"The markets look fine until everyone re-runs their valuation models," Birrell said. "Ultimately, the numbers are the numbers and they've got to come through."
(Reporting by Marc Jones and Naomi Rovnick; editing by Amanda Cooper and Ros Russell)

Title: US business activity hits five-year high but strong demand fuels inflation fears
Article:
WASHINGTON: US business activity raced to a more than five-year high in September, fuelled by a surge in new orders, though strong demand strained supply chains and pushed prices higher.
S&P Global said on Wednesday its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, increased to 58.4 this month.
That was the highest level since July 2021 and followed a reading of 56.0 in August.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. The rise in the PMI reflected strong gains in both the services and manufacturing sectors.
The PMI was consistent with the economy growing at around a 5 per cent annualised rate, S&P Global said.
It also noted a sharp rise in work backlogs and supply chain delays, "pointing to a lack of operating capacity which fed through to higher prices."
The Atlanta Federal Reserve's gross domestic product tracking estimate is running at a 5.1 per cent rate.
The economy grew at a 1.5 per cent pace in the April-June quarter.
"Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
"However, this growth is being accompanied by some of the most severe supply chain bottlenecks seen in the near-two-decade survey history if the pandemic is excluded."
The supply constraints mostly stem from the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its seventh month.
Strong demand adding to inflation
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said on Monday supply shocks were proving more persistent, adding there was evidence that strong demand was now adding to the problem.
That view was supported by the findings of the S&P Global survey.
The survey's measure of new orders received by businesses raced to 58.2, the highest reading since March 2022, from 55.2 in August.
The increase was across both services and manufacturing industries. Incomplete orders, a key indicator of capacity utilisation and future business growth, increased to the highest level since May 2022.
Though companies across manufacturing and services sectors boosted hiring to tackle the order backlog, S&P Global also noted increasing reports of problems finding suitable staff.
"While this accumulation of uncompleted orders bodes well for the further expansion of output and capacity in the coming months, it also indicates that companies are developing more pricing power, and hence is a worry for the inflation outlook," said Williamson.
The survey's gauge of prices paid by businesses for inputs jumped to 66.4, the highest reading since October 2022, from 59.9 in August.
Both services and manufacturing businesses reported higher input prices.
S&P Global noted that high raw materials prices in manufacturing were also often linked to supply shortages.
It said suppliers' delivery times lengthened considerably on average, "with the incidence of supply chain delays the most widespread since July 2022."
A measure of prices paid increased, with the sharpest gain in the services sector.
Further gains are likely as record high diesel prices will, among other things, boost the cost of transporting goods.
The Federal Reserve last week raised its benchmark overnight interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75 per cent — 4.00 per cent range and flagged more hikes in the coming months.

Title: Crew member killed, 27 evacuated after ship targeted near Strait of Hormuz
Article:
ISTANBUL: One crew member was killed and 27 others were evacuated after a commercial vessel was targeted near Oman's Musandam Governorate overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, Omani authorities said Wednesday, Anadolu Ajansi reported.
The Omani Maritime Security Centre said in a statement on the US social media platform X that a Royal Navy of Oman vessel, in coordination with relevant authorities, evacuated the crew of the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged commercial ship Cape Dao.
"Twenty-seven crew members were evacuated and provided with the necessary medical care after the vessel was targeted 2.5 nautical miles off Musandam Governorate," the centre said.
The attack caused a fire in the engine room and killed one crew member, it added.
Hours before the Omani announcement, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said a cargo vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire on board and leaving the ship adrift.
UKMTO did not identify the party responsible for the attack.
Oman's Musandam Governorate lies along the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important waterways for energy shipments and global trade.
Shipping through the waterway has faced disruptions since war broke out in late February between Iran on one side and the US and Israel on the other, amid attacks on commercial vessels and mutual threats over the security of the waterway.

Title: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
Article:
WASHINGTON: The United States and China have agreed to extend by two months a trade truce that was due to expire on November 10, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger trade deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday.
Bessent made the remarks on Fox News hours after his second meeting in four days with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to prepare for a summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
"We met today to see if we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things," the Treasury chief said, noting that the two-month extension of the trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea in May would give the two sides "more time to see what we can do on the economic front."
Bessent told reporters earlier that Beijing had raised the prospect of a more expansive US-China trade deal during 12 hours of talks on Sunday, but gave no details of its potential scope. Wednesday's meeting lasted about 90 minutes, Treasury said.
Asked if a deal could be negotiated by January 10, Bessent told Fox News that was not yet clear, adding Washington was also pressing China to "be a bit more fulsome" in meeting its commitments under the existing deal in coming months.
He said Beijing was meeting its requirement to buy 25 million tons of soybeans, but was lagging on its pledge to buy US$17 billion in other agricultural goods.
US officials last week said the delivery of rare earths by China was also lagging.
Thursday's summit - the second of potentially four meetings between Trump and Xi this year - could see some announcements on the two countries goal of taking tariffs off US$30 billion in non-critical goods, on financial services and agricultural purchases, Bessent said.
"Given that this could be a historic year where the leaders meet up to four times -- this being the second meeting, in Shenzhen and then in Miami -- we're open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement or examining the bigger deal," Bessent told reporters earlier. "We're fine with both, and we're going to do what's best for the American people."
In a post on X, Bessent called the discussions substantive and said Treasury was focused on securing meaningful commitments that protected American workers, farmers and businesses while advancing US economic and national security interests.
Bessent said he met He at the World Bank headquarters in Washington to clear up some "unfinished business" ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, adding that the Trump administration wanted strategic stability based on "reciprocity and fairness."
Bessent, He and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met in New York on Sunday in an effort to tee up potential trade and artificial intelligence agreements for the two leaders to consider. Bessent called those talks successful, saying both sides had agreed to launch a communications "hotline" for notifying each other about AI safety incidents.
China's response to the AI hotline plan was unclear, with state news agency Xinhua acknowledging only that the two sides discussed AI.
US-China analysts say expectations on AI cooperation are low due to a lack of mutual trust on the technology and because neither side has expressed serious interest in slowing down development. In fact, Trump has said the opposite, that he would not "stifle" AI growth and would maintain the US lead over China in what he now calls "super intelligence."
The Busan "economic detente" dramatically lowered bilateral tariff rates that had escalated to triple digits after tit-for-tat retaliation over Trump's tariff hikes last year. China also had agreed to restore the flow of rare earth magnets and other critical minerals that it had severely restricted.

Title: [UPDATED] PN activities suspended, not deregistered - RoS
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Registrar of Societies (RoS) has suspended all activities of Perikatan Nasional (PN) effective yesterday, following a notice issued to the coalition seeking an explanation over a complaint lodged by Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu).
RoS said the suspension was made under subsection 13(2A) of the Societies Act 1966 (Act 832), following the notice issued to PN on Sept 22.
However, the department stressed that the notice was not a decision to cancel PN's registration, but was issued to give the coalition a reasonable period to respond to the complaint.
"RoS issued a notice under subsection 13(2) of the Societies Act 1966 (Act 832) dated Sept 22, 2026, and a reasonable period was given to PN to respond to the notice.
"The notice sought an explanation from PN regarding the complaint lodged by Bersatu with RoS and was not a decision to cancel its registration," it said in a statement today.
RoS said following the notice, it also issued a suspension order on all PN activities effective Sept 23.
It said this was intended to safeguard the interests of the organisation from continuing to breach its constitution.
"RoS urges all parties to refer to official information issued by the department and avoid speculation or the dissemination of unverified information that could cause confusion among the public," it said.
Yesterday, PN confirmed receiving the RoS notice dated Sept 22, which gave the coalition 30 days to explain why its registration should not be cancelled.
A source confirmed that the notice was conveyed to the PN chairman, PN secretary-general and all component parties.
BH also understands that several PN component parties were instructed not to use the coalition's name and logo in any activities until the Registrar of Societies makes a final decision.
RoS had previously confirmed receiving a formal complaint from Bersatu on Aug 11, including allegations that the party was not involved in the PN Supreme Council meeting on July 16 and issues concerning its membership status in the coalition.
Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin was also reported to have called on RoS to make an immediate decision on the complaints lodged by the party, including allegations of eight breaches by the PN leadership.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Pantai hospitals equip Batu Pahat community with burn response skills
Article:
BATU PAHAT: Pantai Hospital Melaka and Pantai Hospital Batu Pahat have equipped residents with practical knowledge on managing burn injuries and responding to fire-related emergencies.
The hospitals brought together healthcare professionals, emergency responders and members of the community for the Burn Awareness Campaign 2026 at Batu Pahat Mall recently.
The campaign focused on helping the public understand what to do in the crucial first few minutes of an emergency, covering burn management, emergency response and fire prevention.
Pantai Hospital Melaka chief executive officer Dr Kevin Khoo said many burn injuries occur during everyday situations, making it important for people to know how to respond quickly and correctly.
"Many burn injuries happen in ordinary, everyday moments, whether at home, in the kitchen, or during a simple accident.
"That is why knowing what to do in those first few minutes matters so much. A calm, correct first response can prevent a burn from becoming more serious and can change the course of a patient's recovery," he said.
He said the hospital treated a wide range of burn cases, from minor injuries to those requiring specialist surgical care.
"Bringing this expertise directly to communities like Batu Pahat helps residents recognise when a burn can be managed at home, and when it's time to seek further medical attention," he added.
The campaign featured health talks by specialists from Pantai Hospital Melaka on the immediate and longer-term management of burn injuries.
Emergency Medicine consultant Dr Teh Yong Hup explained how burn patients are assessed and stabilised in the Emergency Department, including when medical attention is required instead of home treatment.
Plastic and reconstructive surgeon Dr Lee Shi Zhen highlighted the longer-term impact of serious burns, including complications such as burn sepsis and contractures, and the importance of specialist follow-up care.
The campaign also included a fire safety awareness talk by the Penggaram Fire Station on common household fire risks and practical measures families can take to improve home safety.
The Batu Pahat St John Ambulance also conducted CPR demonstrations and provided basic emergency response guidance.
Pantai Hospital Batu Pahat acting chief operating officer Tiong Ngee Zheng said the campaign reflected the hospital's role in supporting the community beyond patient care.
"Batu Pahat is the community we serve every day, and we want our role to extend beyond caring for patients when they come through our doors.
"This allowed us to make practical health information and preventive screenings more accessible to families," he said.

Title: USM takes research beyond the lab
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) has secured RM1.202 million in new industry funding from Intel Malaysia and Micron Memory Malaysia.
This gives fresh momentum to Malaysia's drive to build advanced semiconductor capability, develop highly specialised talent and move university research into industrial application.
At the University Research and Innovation Investment Summit (URIIS) 2026 at the World Trade Centre Kuala Lumpur, USM Vice-Chancellor Professor Datuk Seri Dr Abdul Rahman Mohamed said the funding provides a concrete response to one of Malaysia's most persistent innovation challenges: moving promising university research beyond publications and prototypes into validation, investment, production and wider market adoption.
Opening the summit, Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi identified the critical gap between research and commercial scale as Malaysia's "missing middle".
To close it, he called for three decisive shifts: from relying mainly on grants to building a broader ecosystem of capital; from research outputs to real-world solutions; and from talent to enterprise and ownership.
The challenge is particularly urgent because Malaysia already possesses a formidable innovation base.
The country ranked 34th among 139 economies in the Global Innovation Index 2025 and second among upper-middle-income economies.
Its Malaysian R&D Commercialisation Portal records more than 500 matched patents valued at over RM2 billion, alongside more than 120 active missions.
The strategic task is therefore no longer simply to generate ideas, but to connect the strongest of them with credible partners, patient capital, industrial validation and clear routes to scale.
[[nid:1539834]]
Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir reinforced that imperative, saying URIIS must ultimately be judged by investments secured, technologies licensed, pilot projects launched, partnerships formed and solutions taken to market.
The inaugural summit brought universities, investors, industry and policymakers together around more than 200 investment-potential technologies spanning at least nine strategic sectors.
USM supplied some of the summit's strongest evidence of that model in action.
Intel Malaysia and Micron Memory Malaysia presented RM482,000 and RM720,000,respectively, to Rahman.
The cheque presentation, made by Intel Foundry vice-president and Intel Malaysia managing director Wei Chern Lee and Micron Memory Malaysia CAT assembly engineering director Sia Chen Seng, was witnessed by Zahid and Zambry.
Intel Malaysia was the principal sponsor of the USM pavilion, supported by co-sponsors Micron Memory Malaysia, SanDisk Storage Malaysia and ViTrox Corporation Bhd.
USM was the only public university to mount a dedicated, industry-sponsored pavilion at URIIS, a significant endorsement of its ability to align frontier research, specialised talent and real industrial requirements.
The USM-Intel partnership, established in 2023, has now funded 11 advanced packaging projects worth about RM1.61 million in total, including two new projects this year. It has also produced an industry-aligned elective course, a microprocessor laboratory and a joint Industry-on-Campus facility.
Most notably, USM is the first institution outside the United States to gain access to Intel's 18A Process Design Kit, giving  researchers exceptional exposure to next-generation chip-design technology.
Micron Memory Malaysia's RM720,000 contribution builds on its broader collaboration with USM across semiconductor research and talent development.
The wider partnership has focused on bringing industry knowledge closer to the classroom through initiatives such as the Semiconductor Package Assembly & Test  programme, formerly known as ATMP.
Developed with industry-relevant content and supported by Micron technical experts, the programme helps bridge academic learning with practical semiconductor manufacturing knowledge and strengthens the pipeline of industry-ready engineering talent.
USM also led the Driving Advanced Packaging in Malaysia forum with senior representatives from Intel, ViTrox, FusionAP and Broadcom.
The discussion identified four capabilities that Malaysia must develop in concert: highly skilled local talent, world-class research and development infrastructure, a resilient supply chain, and stronger participation by Malaysian companies and start-ups in higher-value activities.
The university's commercialisation pipeline extended to the investment stage.
Seven USM researchers pitched technologies directly to the Malaysian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association and Leave a Nest, while five researchers presented expertise across semiconductors and advanced materials, sustainable energy, life sciences and health, defence and security, and advanced mobility.
This exposed the technologies to rigorous assessment of market need, readiness, scalability and investment potential.
USM's international reach was strengthened further through an exchange of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Leave a Nest Japan.
Existing collaboration with its network of Japanese companies and investors has generated research, development and investment opportunities estimated at US$120,000, including links with Euglena Co Ltd and KINCHO and access to international innovation platforms.
USM's presence at URIIS 2026 broadened the meaning of commercialisation. Alongside frontier semiconductor research, its COMPASSION framework (Community Programme for Sustainable Impact Mission) showed how communities can become economic partners while retaining ownership of their knowledge.
The work reflects the Leave No One Behind  principle of the United Nations 2030 Agenda by connecting communities to viable markets.
In Baling, COMPASSION is connecting the 276-member Kensiu Orang Asli community's mengkuang weaving traditions to the premium corporate gift market while keeping cultural ownership with the weavers.
At the Centre for Transformation of Persons with Disabilities, a USM and MAIK (Islamic and Malay Custom Council of Kelantan) initiative, tanjak-making training has led to commissioned work. Two of the 28 trainees are now recognised as skilled artisans.
Together, these initiatives show how research can create viable livelihoods while advancing cultural ownership, dignity and inclusion, ensuring that communities have a meaningful stake in the opportunities they help to build on their own terms.
The true significance of URIIS 2026 will be felt long after the summit ends. Malaysia's most meaningful innovation milestones will be measured in transformative technologies adopted, globally competitive enterprises built and greater value retained within the country.
USM has placed itself at the forefront of this defining national ambition. Its next and most important task is to demonstrate that Malaysian research can complete the journey from outstanding discovery to world class industrial capability, and from national promise to global distinction.

Title: The dependent independent director
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Independent directors are expected to provide objective, impartial and independent judgement to the board.
Their role is particularly important because they are supposed to challenge management, scrutinise major decisions, protect shareholders' interests and ensure that the board does not simply become a rubber stamp for executive management or dominant shareholders.
Yet independence on paper does not always translate into independence in practice.
An individual may satisfy the formal definition of an "independent director" while gradually becoming psychologically, financially or socially dependent on the company, its management or controlling shareholders.
This phenomenon can seriously weaken corporate governance.
How does independence become compromised?
Long tenure and familiarity
One of the most common causes is prolonged service on the same board. Over time, an independent director develops close relationships with the chairman, chief executive officer and fellow directors. Familiarity can make difficult questions uncomfortable.
The director may gradually become reluctant to challenge people whom he or she has known for many years.
Professional scepticism can be replaced by trust, and constructive challenge can give way to "we know how things work here."
Dependence on board fees
Although directors' fees are normally modest compared with executive remuneration, they can nevertheless create a psychological dependency, particularly when an individual holds several directorships or relies substantially on board appointments as an important source of income.
The fear of losing the appointment can unconsciously influence behaviour. A director may ask: "Will I still be invited to serve on this board if I oppose management?"
Once that question enters the decision-making process, independence is already under pressure.
Appointment controlled by dominant shareholders
Where a controlling shareholder effectively determines who joins the board, the independent director may feel an obligation to the person who appointed him or her.
This can create a subtle but important conflict. The director's legal and fiduciary responsibilities are to the company, but psychologically the director may feel that loyalty is owed to the controlling shareholder.
Social and personal relationships
Independence can also be compromised through friendships, business relationships, family connections and social networks.
Directors who regularly socialise with senior management may find it difficult to challenge their decisions objectively.
The problem is not necessarily misconduct. Human beings naturally tend to trust and support people with whom they have developed relationships.
Information asymmetry
Management controls much of the information presented to the board. An independent director who depends entirely on management for information can become dependent on management's interpretation of events.
If management presents only selected information, minimises problems or frames alternatives in a particular way, the board may unknowingly become dependent on management's narrative.
Board culture
A powerful chairman or dominant CEO can create a culture in which dissent is discouraged. Directors who repeatedly challenge management may be labelled "difficult", "negative" or "not being a team player".
Over time, some directors learn that agreement is easier than disagreement. The board may then develop groupthink, where maintaining harmony becomes more important than asking uncomfortable questions.
Why does dependency develop?
The fundamental reason is that independence is not merely a structural condition; it is also a behavioural quality.
A director can meet every regulatory test for independence and still lack the courage to exercise independent judgement.
There are also powerful psychological forces at work. Directors may suffer from confirmation bias, preferring information that supports management's existing position.
Familiarity bias can cause them to place excessive trust in people they know well. Reciprocity can create an unconscious sense of obligation toward those who appointed or supported them.
Another factor is the desire to maintain board cohesion. Directors may believe that disagreement damages relationships or undermines the board.
Consequently, they compromise their own views in the interest of consensus.
The consequences
When independent directors become dependent, the board's ability to provide effective oversight deteriorates.
Poor management decisions may go unchallenged. Related-party transactions may receive insufficient scrutiny.
Financial reporting issues may not receive adequate questioning. Risk exposures can be underestimated, and warning signs may be rationalised rather than investigated.
The greatest danger is that the board can appear independent while no longer functioning independently.
This is particularly dangerous for minority shareholders because they rely heavily on independent directors to act as a counterbalance to management and controlling shareholders.
How can independence be strengthened?
Companies should look beyond the formal independence declaration. Boards should periodically assess whether directors demonstrate independent minds, independent judgement and constructive scepticism.
Regular board evaluations should examine whether directors speak up, challenge assumptions, request additional information and disagree when necessary.
Tenure should be monitored, particularly where long service may create excessive familiarity.
Board appointments should also consider whether a director has genuine freedom from relationships that could influence judgement.
Most importantly, independent directors must recognise that their responsibility is not to be popular. Their responsibility is to ask the difficult question when necessary.
A truly independent director should be able to say "no" without fear, "I disagree" without hesitation, and "I need more information" without embarrassment.
Ultimately, independence is not a title conferred upon a director at the time of appointment.
It is a quality that must be demonstrated repeatedly through conduct, judgement and courage throughout the director's tenure.

Title: World's largest sovereign wealth fund holds stake in Northern Solar [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The world's largest sovereign wealth fund holds a stake in ACE Market-listed Northern Solar Holdings Bhd, whose shares crossed RM1 for the first time on Wednesday after extending a blistering three-day run.
Bursa Malaysia data shows Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) holds 10 million Northern Solar shares, or 2.53 per cent. Separately, Norway's Statens pensjonsfond utland is listed with 9.97 million shares, or 2.52 per cent.
NBIM is the investment management arm of Norges Bank, Norway's central bank, and manages the country's Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), also known in Norwegian as Statens pensjonsfond utland.
It is unclear whether the NBIM and Statens pensjonsfond utland entries represent the same or separate holdings.
On a simple aggregation, the two entries amount to 19.97 million shares, equivalent to about 5.05 per cent of Northern Solar. However, Business Times could not establish whether they should be treated as a single interest.
The GPFG was worth NOK22.68 trillion (about US$2.4 trillion) as at end-June 2026, NBIM records show.
It is the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, followed by China's State Administration of Foreign Exchange and China Investment Corporation, according to the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute.
NBIM's investment records show its stake in Northern Solar dates to 2025, although they do not specify when the shares were acquired.
This points to two possibilities: the Norwegian investor either participated in Northern Solar's initial public offering (IPO) or accumulated the shares after its Feb 6, 2025 listing.
Northern Solar's IPO included an offer for sale of 25.71 million existing shares to selected investors through private placement at 63 sen each.
The prospectus did not identify the selected investors.
A Business Times review of NBIM's holdings shows Norges Bank held stakes in 174 Bursa Malaysia-listed companies worth a combined NOK26.32 billion (RM11.33 billion) as at end-June, largely those listed on the Main Market.
Of the total, at least 20 are ACE Market-listed companies, including Southern Score Builders Bhd, Aumas Resources Bhd, Jati Tinggi Group Bhd, Foodie Media Bhd, Pan Merchant Bhd and Pekat Group Bhd.
Its largest stake in a Main Market-listed company was a 5.08 per cent interest in semiconductor company Unisem (M) Bhd.
This was followed by Malaysian Pacific Industries Bhd at 4.82 per cent, Pentamaster Corp Bhd at 4.70 per cent, Mi Technovation Bhd at 4.62 per cent and Dagang NeXchange Bhd at 4.47 per cent.
Meanwhile, Northern Solar's two largest shareholders are managing director Lew Shoong Kai and executive director Chew Win Hoe, who each hold 29.26 per cent, Bursa Malaysia data shows.
Other substantial shareholders are Areca Capital Sdn Bhd with 6.34 per cent and Kenanga Investors Bhd with 5.64 per cent.
Lagenda Properties Bhd holds 4.87 per cent, followed by Kenanga Islamic Investors Bhd with 3.79 per cent and Hong Leong Asset Management Bhd with 3.42 per cent.
At Wednesday's market close, Northern Solar shares were up 8.51 per cent or eight sen at RM1.02, valuing the company at RM403.51 million.
The stock had climbed as much as 21.28 per cent or 20 sen to an intraday high of RM1.14 earlier in the session.
Northern Solar's latest gains extend a sharp run that began after the government unveiled measures last week to accelerate corporate renewable energy adoption under the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme.
The stock rose 9.42 per cent to 75.5 sen on Monday before surging another 22.88 per cent to 94 sen on Tuesday.
At RM1.02, Northern Solar has gained 52.24 per cent or 35 sen from its 67 sen close last Friday, adding about RM138.5 million to its market capitalisation.
On Sept 1, the company said it had received the Securities Commission's approval to transfer its listing from the ACE Market to the Main Market of Bursa Malaysia. It expects to complete the transfer by year-end.
Northern Solar was listed at 63 sen a share and closed its first trading day 25.4 per cent higher at 79 sen.
Based in Petaling Jaya, the firm is principally involved in the engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) of solar photovoltaic systems, renewable energy generation and operation and maintenance services.
EPCC remains its core business, contributing RM37.4 million, or 98.1 per cent, of the group's RM38.2 million revenue for the first quarter ended June 30, 2026, its highest quarterly revenue since listing and up 36.1 per cent from a year earlier.
Net profit stood at RM3.97 million, up 3.12 per cent from RM3.85 million.

Title: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal
Article:
WASHINGTON: The United States and China have agreed to extend by two months a trade truce that was due to expire on Nov 10, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger trade deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday.
Bessent made the remarks on Fox News hours after his second meeting in four days with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to prepare for a summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
"We met today to see if we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things," the Treasury chief said, noting that the two-month extension of the trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in May would give the two sides "more time to see what we can do on the economic front."
Bessent told reporters earlier that Beijing had raised the prospect of a more expansive US-China trade deal during 12 hours of talks on Sunday, but gave no details of its potential scope. Wednesday's meeting lasted about 90 minutes, Treasury said.
Asked if a deal could be negotiated by Jan 10, Bessent told Fox News that was not yet clear, adding Washington was also pressing China to "be a bit more fulsome" in meeting its commitments under the existing deal in coming months.
He said Beijing was meeting its requirement to buy 25 million tons of soybeans, but was lagging on its pledge to buy $17 billion in other agricultural goods.
US officials last week said the delivery of rare earths by China was also lagging.
Thursday's summit — the second of potentially four meetings between Trump and Xi this year — could see some announcements on the two countries' goal of taking tariffs off $30 billion in non-critical goods, on financial services and agricultural purchases, Bessent said.
"Given that this could be a historic year where the leaders meet up to four times — this being the second meeting, in Shenzhen and then in Miami — we're open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement or examining the bigger deal," Bessent told reporters earlier. "We're fine with both, and we're going to do what's best for the American people."
In a post on X, Bessent called the discussions substantive and said Treasury was focused on securing meaningful commitments that protected American workers, farmers and businesses while advancing US economic and national security interests.
Bessent said he met He at the World Bank headquarters in Washington to clear up some "unfinished business" ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, adding that the Trump administration wanted strategic stability based on "reciprocity and fairness."
Bessent, He and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met in New York on Sunday in an effort to tee up potential trade and artificial intelligence agreements for the two leaders to consider. Bessent called those talks successful, saying both sides had agreed to launch a communications "hotline" for notifying each other about AI safety incidents.
China's response to the AI hotline plan was unclear, with state news agency Xinhua acknowledging only that the two sides discussed AI.
US-China analysts say expectations on AI cooperation are low due to a lack of mutual trust on the technology and because neither side has expressed serious interest in slowing down development. In fact, Trump has said the opposite, that he would not "stifle" AI growth and would maintain the US lead over China in what he now calls "super intelligence."
The Busan "economic detente" dramatically lowered bilateral tariff rates that had escalated to triple digits after tit-for-tat retaliation over Trump's tariff hikes last year. China also had agreed to restore the flow of rare earth magnets and other critical minerals that it had severely restricted.

Title: Airstrike hits Afghanistan's Kandahar city
Article:
AFGHANISTAN: An airstrike hit the southern Afghan city of Kandahar on Thursday, home to the Taliban government's supreme leader, a resident told AFP.
The resident heard a jet, then a large explosion, and saw a fire in the centre of the city.
Afghanistan's military and government officials did not immediately respond to AFP requests to comment on the strike, which comes days after a deadly Pakistani bombardment in the border area.
At least three civilians were killed in the strikes on eastern Afghanistan, the United Nations reported, which Pakistan said killed 28 militants.
Although there have been multiple such attacks in the border area, strikes on Afghan cities are rare.
Both Kandahar and the capital Kabul were hit when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war in late February, with weeks of violence killing hundreds of Afghan civilians, according to the UN mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA).
Although a ceasefire was agreed in March, mediation from several countries has failed to produce a lasting resolution between the neighbours.
Security issues have proved a sticking point, especially Pakistan's demand that Afghanistan curb the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militant group.
Islamabad accuses the Taliban government of sheltering militants behind a surge in attacks, particularly the TTP, which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years.
Afghan officials deny the charge and counter that Pakistan harbours hostile groups and does not respect its sovereignty.
The Pakistani strikes on the border area this week followed an attack on a police headquarters in northern Pakistan on Friday that killed at least 31 people.
The attack was claimed by a group which is linked to the TTP.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: North Korean IT contractor found working remotely in New Zealand
Article:
WELLINGTON: A North Korean IT worker used a fake identity to obtain remote work with a New Zealand company and then threatened to release sensitive information when exposed, Wellington's cybersecurity agency said Thursday.
New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre said the IT contractor was working remotely for a large New Zealand business, which grew "suspicious" of his true identity over time.
"Investigation identified the worker as being from North Korea," the report said.
"The North Korean worker used a false persona including fake identity documents, a New Zealand address as a contact point and recruited a New Zealand citizen to receive and operate the company's laptop."
On learning the contractor's true identity, the business ended their employment and refused to pay for their services.
The worker then "claimed to have obtained commercially sensitive information and threatened to release this if not paid," the report added.
North Korea faces a slew of international sanctions over its weapons and nuclear programmes, which ban its citizens from being issued work visas abroad among a litany of other restrictions.
In July, the United States and 10 Asian and European allies warned companies against employing North Korean IT workers whose labour was generating crucial foreign currency to fund that nuclear weapons programme.
North Korea has furiously denied those allegations.
"In some cases, the workers also undertake malicious cyber operations. These workers often operate under front companies overseen by the North Korean state apparatus," New Zealand's Cyber Security Centre said.
The report urged businesses to interview potential contractors face-to-face to mitigate the risk of clandestine activities.
The 48-page risk assessment said 23 per cent of major cyber attacks on New Zealand last year were state-sponsored, naming China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as countries that had launched attacks.
It also warned of an increasing risk to the South Pacific, citing "state-sponsored cyber espionage targeting governments and infrastructure" in the region.

Title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Iowa newspaper and pollster
Article:
WASHINGTON: An Iowa judge, citing First Amendment protections, dismissed President Donald Trump's lawsuit filed in late 2024 against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer over a poll that showed the Republican leader trailing before the 2024 elections.
"At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability," Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said in the ruling on Wednesday.
Trump, who has repeatedly clashed with the media in and outside of court, won the 2024 election.
The ruling in the Register case came as another judge told a hearing that Trump's decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House did not appear to comply with prior rulings by a federal appellate court.
Trump had criticised a poll published on Nov 2, 2024, that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him by three percentage points in Iowa.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Wednesday ruling.
Free speech group FIRE, which represented Selzer, welcomed the ruling.
"We're pleased that the court recognised what we've said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought," FIRE chief counsel Bob Corn-Revere said in a statement.
Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop news programmes he dislikes, called on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavoured broadcast stations of their licences, filed several lawsuits against media outlets and banned some media outlets from the White House.
The US Constitution's First Amendment grants protections for free speech and a free press.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Colombia president orders troops to violence-hit Caribbean city
Article:
SANTA MARTA, (Colombia): Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella sent troops into the Caribbean city of Santa Marta on Tuesday after gunmen attacked shops and burnt vehicles following the killing of one of their leaders.
Videos shared online showed members of the self-styled Conquering Self-Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN) riding through the city on motorbikes, firing on businesses that remained open despite the group announcing a 48-hour curfew.
Santa Marta acts as a gateway to Tayrona National Park, a popular tourist destination overlooking the Caribbean.
AFP journalists saw a truck ablaze in the middle of a road and a charred bus on another street.
Dozens of shops were shuttered and parts of the city were deserted.
The chaos followed an earlier announcement by De la Espriella that the police and air force had killed 13 members of the ACSN, an armed group with roots in Colombia's now-defunct paramilitary movement that lives off extortion and cocaine trafficking.
The president said that the 13 "narcoterrorists" killed included the ACSN's second-in-command, who went by the alias "Cholo."
De la Espriella said in a later video statement that he had ordered "that Santa Marta be militarised."
Following the military operation against the ACSN, "these criminals are trying to set a large part of the Caribbean region on fire," he said, adding that "anyone who does not submit will be taken down."
De la Espriella said on X that he had arrived in Santa Marta to oversee the crackdown.
- Prison or tomb -
Army troops were deployed along the highway that connects the city with the La Guajira department on the Venezuelan border, where ACSN also operates.
US-backed millionaire De la Espriella pledged a heavy hand against Colombia's myriad drug-running groups — from dissident members of the defunct Marxist rebel army FARC to the former paramilitary groups set up to fight the guerrillas — when he took office in August.
He has ordered bombing raids on guerrilla camps in several parts of the country and held press conferences next to the corpses of rebels laid out in body bags.
"Cholo" is the second senior ACSN member to be killed by the security forces in less than a month, after another commander, "Bendito Menor," was killed in La Guajira.
The ACSN is one of the many armed groups that De la Espriella's leftist predecessor Gustavo Petro had engaged in failed peace talks with.
The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace in Colombia estimates the group has around 800 members.
De la Espriella has ended all dialogue with armed groups and vowed to put them either "in prison or a tomb," with the help of the United States. — AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Son of Israel's US envoy injured in West Bank ramming attack
Article:
RAMALLAH: Israeli ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter said his son was the soldier injured in a car-ramming attack on Wednesday in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli police said earlier a Palestinian man drove a car at high speed towards a policewoman and a soldier who were conducting vehicle searches at an intersection near the Israeli settlement of Beit Horon west of Ramallah.
"As a result, the soldier was wounded and is currently receiving medical treatment. The attacker was killed by the forces," the police added.
Israel's Magen David Adom emergency services said its teams had evacuated a man in serious condition to hospital.
Ambassador Leiter said his son was the injured soldier, adding: "Neria needs a miracle."
"Neria continued to serve in the reserves after losing his older brother, Moshe Yedidya Leiter," he added on X, referring to another son who was killed in action in Gaza in November 2023.
Israeli politicians responded with words of support.
"My wife Sara and I, together with all the people of Israel, are praying for a miracle," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a post on X.
Israel's public broadcaster Kan reported that the ambassador was meant to attend Netanyahu's speech at the UN General Assembly on Thursday, but was instead flying back to Israel to see his son.
Netanyahu's office said the prime minister visited Neria Leiter in the hospital before departing for the United States.
The statement said Leiter was "very seriously wounded" in the attack.
The Palestinian Health Ministry said it had been informed of the death of 29-year-old Mahmoud Mohammad Mahmoud Suleiman, "who was shot by Israeli forces near the village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah."
It added that Israeli authorities were withholding his body.
Beit Ur al-Tahta mayor Hazem Suleiman, who is not related to Mahmoud Suleiman, told AFP that Israeli forces raided the village and searched the man's family home.
"The town is closed off, with all its entrances blocked. There is no social or commercial activity, and no signs of normal life," he said, adding that the army had also searched other houses.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and violence there has surged since Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war.
On Sunday, an Israeli settler was shot dead in the West Bank, with the military saying it had arrested the suspected gunman.
That same day, Israel's military also reported an attempted car-ramming in the West Bank, in which the perpetrator was killed.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian Health Ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,110 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war.
Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: UK air force fighter jet crashes on training exercise
Article:
LONDON: UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting on Wednesday said an investigation was underway after an air force Hawk fighter jet crashed during a training exercise in north Wales.
A video clip posted on social media showed what appeared to be the two pilots ejecting moments before the aircraft nosedived and crashed in flames.
The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the Royal Air Force (RAF) Valley station on Anglesey, an island off the northwest coast of Wales.
"On take-off there was an orange flame and as it accelerated it was basically on fire," a witness told the regional news website North Wales Live.
Streeting, speaking at a conference in London, said the pair were being treated in hospital "and of course we're investigating how and why this happened."
The pilots are believed to have suffered minor injuries, according to police.
The RAF added on X that it had decided "to temporarily pause Hawk T1 and T2 operations as a precautionary measure whilst investigations are ongoing."
The Hawk T1 and newer T2 versions are transonic, two-seat training aircraft used to train fast jet pilots.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: PH Plus seen as possible lifeline for Bersatu in Melaka [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: An electoral understanding under the Pakatan Harapan Plus framework may be the most practical path forward for Bersatu following its split with Pas.
Universiti Malaya political analyst Dr Mohammad Tawfik Yaakub said Bersatu was likely to explore new electoral arrangements as going solo  would be a high-risk option.
He said  making a new pact was a priority to avoid isolation and prevent multi-cornered contests from eroding its support.
"A PH Plus arrangement may be the most practical avenue if formal cooperation with Pas is no longer possible," he said.
"However, this depends on whether both sides can agree on a limited, seat-by-seat understanding rather than a full political alliance."
On Saturday, Melaka PH said  it was finalising negotiations with parties that shared similar aspirations, including Bersatu, to form a PH Plus collaboration to contest the Melaka election.
Melaka PH chairman Adly Zahari said the negotiations were being conducted based on decisions made at a  PH presidential council meeting.
"The negotiations also included Bersatu, but any form of cooperation will only be announced after the negotiation process has been completed," he  said.
[[nid:1539785]]
Tawfik said cooperation with Barisan Nasional remained unlikely given their direct competition for Malay support and unresolved political differences.
"Retaining its (single) seat will be difficult if Bersatu faces Pas, BN and PH separately. Its advantage will depend heavily on the strength of local candidates, incumbency, grassroots machinery, and whether Malay votes are fragmented among several blocs."
As for  other seats, he said that would only be realistic if Bersatu secured an electoral pact or a strategic understanding that prevented three- or four-cornered fights.
"Without such mechanisms, the contest will descend into a battle of machinery, local credibility and vote consolidation."
While contesting under its own logo remains an option, Tawfik said  Bersatu carried significant electoral risk.
"Bersatu may, therefore, prefer a selective electoral pact, potentially under the PH Plus framework, to protect strategic seats and reduce vote-splitting.
"The main issue is whether such an arrangement can be accepted by PH supporters and Bersatu's grassroots without causing backlash or weakening campaign mobilisation."
Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities Associate Professor Dr Mazlan Ali said PH Plus could be an ideal choice because, apart from PH, no political party or coalition was equal in strength to BN and Pas.
"I believe Bersatu will establish ties with other coalitions to boost its strength and chances of winning, because contesting solo would split votes.
"PH is the best option for Bersatu in the Melaka  election."
[[nid:1539784]]
He added that Bersatu had a 50-50 chance of retaining the Sungai Udang seat and winning back Bemban but with PH, it would stand a better chance.
Bersatu won both seats in the previous election, but its Bemban assemblyman was later expelled from the party.
"I do not expect Bersatu to win more seats unless it is a  fight involving BN, Pas and PH."
Melaka will hold its 16th election soon following the dissolution of the state assembly yesterday.
The Melaka assembly has 28 seats, with BN having won 21 in the previous election.
